title: Love Liza
full_review:
A grief-stricken husband unravels after the unexpected suicide of his young wife in "Love Liza" (Sony Classics).

Philip Seymour Hoffman graduates from fine character actor to his first starring role in this labor of love, written by his brother Gordy Hoffman and directed by his friend, Todd Louiso. The actor is affecting as the devastated widower numbed by the shock and unwilling to just get on with life. However, the film is flawed in focusing solely on his character's misery without giving viewers any idea about the past life of the husband and wife. It's like watching a relationship story in a vacuum.

Co-workers tiptoe around Web designer Wilson Joel (Hoffman), whose unpredictable outbursts or glowering silences unnerve everyone. His mother-in-law (Kathy Bates, sporting a severe crew cut) tries to be supportive but her patience wanes when she sees her daughter Liza left a suicide note addressed to him -- but he refuses to open it.

Seeking frequent oblivion, Wilson turns to substance abuse in a form reminiscent of his wife's carbon monoxide poisoning in the garage: He takes to sniffing gasoline fumes. He's able to buy gallons of the stuff since feigning an interest in flying remote-control model airplanes with well-meaning eccentric Denny (Jack Kehler).

But Wilson's inner rage, survivor guilt and fear that he somehow may have triggered his wife's suicide drive him to continue getting high, and he goes so far as to offer spare gasoline to a teen-age couple with the same addiction.

Returning from a road trip to a model-plane competition, Wilson gets a new job offer and has it out with his angry mother-in-law before deciding to read the letter signed "Love, Liza" -- and act on its contents.
The small-scale film captures the protagonist's tortured mental state, but his helping two adolescents get high seems out of character, considering his total self-absorption, and makes him considerably less sympathetic.
As we know no more about him at the film's deliberately ambiguous conclusion, or the reason for his wife's death, the movie is ultimately unsatisfying and has scant emotional resonance. It may accomplish moving Hoffman from featured player to leading man, but the underwritten script leaves too many unanswered questions.

Due to instances of substance abuse also involving minors, brief violence, fleeting shadowy nudity, intermittent rough language and minimal profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
